description: Behavior parity vectors for expressionRuntimeVersion 2 — the value-domain extension (number | string | ref | list), the list/aggregate/membership family, polymorphic Equals, kind predicates, lambda binding (Filter/ListMap/ForEach), Matches over the pinned RE2-compatible XSD-regex subset, NameBasedUuid, the RFC 9562 version 5 UUID of a name (1.2.0), StartsWith, a prefix test of one string by another (1.3.0), and EpochMilliseconds and EpochDays, a date-time or a date read as the whole milliseconds or days since 1970-01-01 (1.4.0). Runs IN ADDITION to expression-vectors.json (v1), every vector of which must pass unchanged under a v2 kernel — that file is the numeric-regression gate. `expected` and `env` values are Values: JSON numbers, strings, arrays (lists), and {"ref": "publisher/package/name"} objects (refs). Normative list-family semantics are the SDK reference engine's: Sum on empty = 0; Min/Max/Average on empty = loud error; Count type-agnostic; absence is the empty list; predicates fail closed on type-confused operands, computations fail loud.

vectors.description: UriLiteral is a kernel-known literal in v2: it evaluates to its ref identity
The caller's resolve may return any Value — here a list
Absence is the empty list; Count of absence is 0
A scalar source promotes to a one-element list (the reference-engine rule)
Numbers stringify per the ECMAScript rule RFC 8785 pins (1 not 1.0; 2.5 stays 2.5)
Refs compare by canonical versionless URI identity — the tx.Equals rule
The string "1" is not the number 1 — cross-kind equality is false, never an error
A URI is never equal to the string spelling of it
A list is a container, not a comparable value
0 is a value, not absence
IsString/IsNumber/IsReference/IsList each recognize their own kind
No kind predicate accepts a foreign kind
A body list flattens; an empty body list contributes nothing (absence = skip)
A VarRef naming anything but an enclosing loopVar is still the caller's leaf
fn:matches semantics — unanchored; authors write ^…$ for whole-string
Flag prefix (?i) at position 0 — the only flag mechanism in the subset
All three prefix flags together — distinct flags in one prefix are in subset
A repeated prefix flag is out of subset — the JS engine rejects (?ii) at compile time while the Go, Python and Rust engines accept it, so the subset decides rather than the host
Only ONE whole-pattern prefix — a second (?s) is a mid-pattern group construct
Mid-pattern flag groups are not portable (JS/Python engines) — out of subset

PINNED counting unit: an astral character (surrogate pair in UTF-16 hosts) is ONE code point — 'a🧬b' is exactly 3 under .{3}. A port counting code units sees 4 and must fail this vector, not the tenant.
One astral character matches a single `.`
The minLength lowering shape over astral input: 3 code points satisfies minLength 3 in every port
A bare `{` that is not a quantifier is engine-divergent (lenient-literal in some, error in others) — the subset requires escaping it
PINNED: \d is [0-9] by textual expansion — Arabic-Indic digits do not match (Rust/Python native \d would say yes; every port must expand)
PINNED: \s is ASCII whitespace by textual expansion — NBSP does not match (native JS \s would say yes; every port must expand)
PINNED: \b is the ASCII word boundary — é is not a word character, so \bé finds no boundary (Unicode \b engines would match; Rust uses (?-u:\b), Python re.ASCII)
In-class shorthand splices as a fragment: [\d-] is [0-9-]
In-class \b is backspace in JS but an error in RE2-family engines — rejected
PINNED: non-dotAll `.` is any code point except \n — it MATCHES \r (the RE2/Python/Go norm; JS and Java engines exclude more line terminators natively and must translate `.` to [^\n])
PINNED: \v is the vertical tab U+000B (Java's native \v is a vertical-whitespace CLASS and must translate to \x0B)
PINNED: (?i) is Unicode simple case folding — é folds to É (Java adds UNICODE_CASE; C# uses CultureInvariant; Python must NOT pass re.ASCII, which disables it)
Ordering comparisons are predicates: non-numeric operands yield 0, never an error
Computations fail loud: Add of a string is a type error, never a coercion
The sh:minCount lowering shape: Count(values) >= 1
The sh:in lowering shape: every value a member of the closed set (Filter misses = 0)
explain() over a list operator: children = the source trace

runtime#25: a caller-resolved leaf inside a Filter body reads the loop element. The caller's PropertyRead evaluates its readSource through the handed-back evaluate, which MUST carry the enclosing loopVar frame — the binding is the kernel's, the read is the caller's

ListMap body = a caller leaf over the loop element; the element bound by loopVar is whatever the caller put in the list — for a host graph, a ref — so readSource evaluating to a ref is the shape every port must handle. The trace shows the caller leaf as a leaf with its resolved value
ForEach over a caller leaf: a multi-valued read contributes each value, a single-valued read contributes itself
The reference engine's convention, pinned INSIDE a loop body so every port's caller leaf agrees: a property with several values reads as a list
A property with one value reads as that value, NOT a one-element list — Equals against the scalar holds (a port wrapping singles in a list fails cross-kind here)
A property with no value reads as the empty list (absence), never an error and never null: Count is 0 for the element without an owner
IsSet over a caller leaf distinguishes the element that has the property
Nested iterators binding the SAME loopVar name: the innermost binder wins, and that precedence reaches a caller leaf too. Were the outer 'it' visible, the inner count would be [0, 2]

A loopVar whose name collides with a name the CALLER binds ('it' is in env as item-1): inside the body the kernel's binding wins — silently, which is why a generator should refuse the collision where it is visible — while outside the body the caller's binding is untouched. size(env.it)=10 + count-of-size-20-elements=1

runtime#26: the trace↔expression contract for an IteratingExpression. children[0] is the source trace; body trace k pairs with element k of the source value — EVERY element, including the one the predicate rejects (value 0): the trace is truthful about what ran, so "which element failed" is positional. What was read (readProp) is on the paired expression node, not repeated here

The coercion hole in the pairing rule: a source that resolves to ONE value (the caller convention: one → itself) is iterated as a one-element list, but the source trace carries the SCALAR. So the rule is "element k of the source value coerced to a list" — a consumer indexing children[0].value directly indexes a scalar. Pinned here so no port and no consumer gets it wrong

runtime#61: a property named after a member every object inherits, such as valueOf, as transformations declares, reads only what the node holds. A node without it reads as absent, the empty list, never the inherited member
RFC 9562 version 5 of www.example.com under the RFC's DNS namespace, as Python's uuid.uuid5 gives it; uuidFormat absent is canonical text
A versionless URI under the RFC's URL namespace: the identifier of a declaration derived from its name
uuidFormat canonical-uuid, named, gives what its absence gives
uuidFormat hex-uuid: the same 32 lower-case hex digits, without hyphens
A namespace's hex digits are read in either case (RFC 9562, section 4), and the result is always lower-case
The name is hashed as its UTF-8 bytes: two-byte, three-byte and an astral four-byte character, never UTF-16 code units
An empty name hashes the namespace's 16 bytes alone
Both operands are expressions: the name here is a bound variable
A namespace that isn't a UUID is an error, never a value
Only canonical text is a namespace: the 32 digits without hyphens are refused, though some UUID parsers accept them
A braced namespace is refused, though some UUID parsers accept it
A urn:uuid: namespace is refused, though some UUID parsers accept it
A namespace with a trailing newline is refused: a pattern whose $ matches before a final newline, as Python's, Java's and .NET's do, would accept it
Hex digits are ASCII only: a fullwidth digit, which a Unicode-aware digit class or number parse reads as 8, is refused
A namespace that isn't a string is an error
A reference is not the string spelling of its URI, so it isn't a namespace
A name that isn't a string is an error
A list is not a name, even of one string
Absence, the empty list, is not a name
A uuidFormat other than canonical-uuid or hex-uuid is an error
A uuidFormat that names a member every object inherits misses, as any other unknown format does
A prefix test, not a substring test: the string must begin with it
A string starts with itself
Every string starts with the empty string, the empty string included
No case folding
Code point by code point, with no Unicode normalization: a decomposed e-acute does not start with the precomposed one
A prefix may end before a combining mark: code points, not grapheme clusters
A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is one code point
A predicate fails closed: a number is not a string
A URI is never the string spelling of it
A list is a container, not a string
The whole milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z
The local time is UTC plus the zone's offset, so the instant is the same as in UTC
+14:00 is the widest offset XSD allows
A fraction finer than a millisecond is floored, so every port gives the same whole number
-0.5 ms floors toward the earlier instant, -1, never toward zero
24:00:00 is the first instant of the next day
24:00:00 may carry a fraction of zeros
2000 is divisible by 400, so it has a 29 February
Year 0 is 1 BCE in XSD 1.1's proleptic Gregorian calendar
-0000 is in the lexical form, and names year 0
Year -1 is the year before year 0
The latest instant whose count is at most 2^53 - 1, its sub-millisecond digit floored
Read as numbers, two date-times order as their instants do
09:00 at +01:00 is 08:00 in UTC, before 08:30 in UTC, though its text sorts after
The instant of a date-time without a time zone is indeterminate
A $ that matches before a final newline would accept this
XSD 1.1's seconds stop at 59
2100 is divisible by 100 and not by 400
Leading zeros only bring a year up to four digits
Only the ASCII digits 0-9 are digits here, never a class such as \d that admits others
A count past 2^53 - 1 is refused, since a number no longer holds every whole value there
Times 86400000 its day count wraps in 64 bits to -8000751616, a count in range: refused before multiplying
Times 86400000 its day count wraps in 64 bits to 793450008870912, a count in range: refused before multiplying
Absence is the empty list, which isn't a date-time: a value that may be absent is guarded with IsSet
A date's time zone is read and ignored, so it counts the day as written
Year 0 is divisible by 400, so it's a leap year
-4 is divisible by 4, so it's a leap year
The order that a LessThan over the two strings can never give
-100 is divisible by 100 and not by 400
